claim: In the dorsal thorax of Drosophila, rows of mechanosensory organs originate from the division of sensory organ progenitor (SOPs).
source: In the dorsal thorax of Drosophila, rows of mechanosensory organs originate from the division of sensory organ progenitor (SOPs).
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the biological system studied, supported by established knowledge of Drosophila development.

claim: In each row of the notum, an anteromedial located central SOP divides first, then neighbouring SOPs divide in a centrifugal wave pattern.
source: We show that in each row of the notum, an anteromedial located central SOP divides first, then neighbouring SOPs divide, and so on.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data presented in Figure 1 and Video 1, showing the temporal and spatial pattern of SOP divisions.

claim: The centrifugal wave of mitoses depends on cell-cell inhibitory interactions mediated by SOP cytoplasmic protrusions.
source: This centrifugal wave of mitoses depends on cell-cell inhibitory interactions mediated by SOP cytoplasmic protrusions and Scabrous, a secreted protein interacting with the Delta/Notch complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that manipulation of protrusions (rac1N17 overexpression) affects the mitotic wave, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The centrifugal wave of mitoses depends on Scabrous, a secreted protein interacting with the Delta/Notch complex.
source: This centrifugal wave of mitoses depends on cell-cell inhibitory interactions mediated by SOP cytoplasmic protrusions and Scabrous, a secreted protein interacting with the Delta/Notch complex.
evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments with scaBP2 mutants and RNAi knockdown showing altered mitotic wave patterns, as presented in Figure 3.

claim: When the mitotic wave was reduced, axonal growth was more synchronous.
source: Furthermore, when this mitotic wave was reduced, axonal growth was more synchronous, axonal terminals had a complex branching pattern and fly behaviour was impaired.
evidence: This is supported by axon length measurements at 24 hr APF in control and scaBP2 pupae shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: When the mitotic wave was reduced, axonal terminals had a complex branching pattern.
source: Furthermore, when this mitotic wave was reduced, axonal growth was more synchronous, axonal terminals had a complex branching pattern and fly behaviour was impaired.
evidence: This is supported by MCFO labeling data showing increased branching in RNAi-sca conditions, as presented in Figure 4C-D.

claim: When the mitotic wave was reduced, fly behaviour was impaired.
source: Furthermore, when this mitotic wave was reduced, axonal growth was more synchronous, axonal terminals had a complex branching pattern and fly behaviour was impaired.
evidence: This is supported by cleaning reflex assay data showing that flies with disrupted mitotic waves require more air puffs to elicit a response, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: The temporal order of progenitor divisions influences the birth order of sensory neurons.
source: We show that the temporal order of progenitor divisions influences the birth order of sensory neurons, axon branching and impact on grooming behaviour.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between mitotic wave timing and axon length measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: The temporal order of progenitor divisions influences axon branching.
source: We show that the temporal order of progenitor divisions influences the birth order of sensory neurons, axon branching and impact on grooming behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that disruption of the mitotic wave leads to altered axon terminal morphology, as shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The temporal order of progenitor divisions impacts grooming behaviour.
source: We show that the temporal order of progenitor divisions influences the birth order of sensory neurons, axon branching and impact on grooming behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data showing impaired cleaning reflex when the mitotic wave is disrupted, as presented in Figure 5.

claim: Developmental timing controls axon wiring neural diversity.
source: These data support the idea that developmental timing controls axon wiring neural diversity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined observations of mitotic wave timing, axon morphology, and behavior.

claim: In the dorsal region of the thorax (notum), SOPs appear sequentially from five parallel proneural rows: first rows 5, followed by rows 1 and 3 and finally rows 2 and 4.
source: In the dorsal region of the thorax (notum), SOPs appear sequentially from five parallel proneural rows: first rows 5, followed by rows 1 and 3 and finally rows 2 and 4 (Usui and Kimura, 1993; Corson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Usui and Kimura, 1993 and Corson et al., 2017.

claim: SOPs selection involves Notch-dependent lateral inhibition from 6 to 12 hr after pupal formation (APF).
source: SOPs selection involves Notch-dependent lateral inhibition from 6 to 12 hr after pupal formation (APF).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila SOP development.

claim: At 16.5 hr APF, SOPs resume the cell cycle and divide to generate a posterior secondary precursor cell (pIIa) and an anterior secondary precursor cell (pIIb).
source: Then, at 16.5 hr APF, SOPs resume the cell cycle and divide to generate a posterior secondary precursor cell (pIIa) and an anterior secondary precursor cell (pIIb).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila SOP development.

claim: After subsequent asymmetric cell divisions, pIIa and pIIb give rise to the external (the socket and the shaft cells) and internal (the neuron, the sheath, and the glial cell) cells respectively.
source: After subsequent asymmetric cell divisions, they give rise to the external (the socket and the shaft cells) and internal (the neuron, the sheath, and the glial cell) cells respectively (Gho et al., 1999; Fichelson and Gho, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Gho et al., 1999 and Fichelson and Gho, 2003.

claim: During organogenesis, the bipolar neurons project their dendrite toward the base of the bristle, and their axons toward the ventral thoracic ganglion.
source: During organogenesis, the bipolar neurons project their dendrite toward the base of the bristle, and their axons toward the ventral thoracic ganglion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila mechanosensory neuron development.

claim: The axons enter the ganglion through the posterior dorsal mesothoracic nerve root and extend branches anteriorly and posteriorly.
source: The axons enter the ganglion through the posterior dorsal mesothoracic nerve root and extend branches anteriorly and posteriorly (Ghysen, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Ghysen, 1980.

claim: The microchætes from earlier born rows are more branched and arborised over a greater area within the neuropil than those from later born rows.
source: Thus, the microchætes form the earlier born rows are more branched and arborised over a greater area within the neuropil than those from later born rows (Ghysen, 1980; Usui-Ishihara and Simpson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Ghysen, 1980 and Usui-Ishihara and Simpson, 2005.

claim: In adult flies, mechanical stimulation of thoracic bristles induces a cleaning reflex in which the first or third leg sweeps the stimulated area.
source: In adult flies, mechanical stimulation of thoracic bristles induces a cleaning reflex in which the first or third leg sweeps the stimulated area.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila behavior.

claim: The cleaning reflex requires the correct connectivity of the bristle neurons.
source: This reflex requires the correct connectivity of the bristle neurons (Corfas and Dudai, 1989; Ghysen, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Corfas and Dudai, 1989 and Ghysen, 1980.

claim: Scabrous is a secreted fibrinogen like protein that interacts physically with N and Dl and modulates their activities.
source: Scabrous is a secreted fibrinogen like protein that interacts physically with N and Dl and modulates their activities (Mok et al., 2005),
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Mok et al., 2005.

claim: In the notum, sca mutants have an excess of bristles, a phenocopy of N mutants, indicating that Sca positively modulates N-activity.
source: Thus, in the notum, sca mutants have an excess of bristles, a phenocopy of N mutants, indicating that Sca positively modulates N-activity (Renaud and Simpson, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Renaud and Simpson, 2001.

claim: In wing discs, ectopic expression of sca inhibits N-pathway by reducing the interactions with its ligands.
source: In wing discs, ectopic expression of sca inhibits N-pathway by reducing the interactions with its ligands (Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Lee et al., 2000.

claim: The first cell in each row to divide (SOP0) was located in the anteromedial region of each row.
source: We observed that the SOP0 cells were located in the anteromedial region of each row and generally, the more distant a SOP was from its corresponding SOP0, the later it divided (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1A-B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1.

claim: The more distant a SOP was from its corresponding SOP0, the later it divided.
source: We observed that the SOP0 cells were located in the anteromedial region of each row and generally, the more distant a SOP was from its corresponding SOP0, the later it divided (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1A-B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1.

claim: All SOPs in a row divided in two hours for all rows analysed.
source: Thus, all SOPs in a row divided in two hours for all rows analysed (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of division timing shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: No statistical difference was found between the rate of the mitotic waves in rows 1, 2, and 3.
source: No statistical difference was found between the rate of the mitotic waves in rows 1, 2, and 3 (p = 0.3954, ANOVA)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of the mitotic wave rates across different rows.

claim: No statistical difference was found between left and right rows.
source: or between left and right rows (p = 0.3038, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing left and right sides of the notum.

claim: No statistical difference was found between the rates of the anterior and posterior mitotic waves.
source: Still, no statistical difference was found between the rates of the anterior and posterior mitotic waves (p = 0.0689, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing anterior and posterior wave propagation.

claim: For control conditions, the mean rate of the mitotic wave is 3.14 µm min–1.
source: For control conditions, this gives for the mean rate 3.14 µm min–1 (see Figure 1 and ).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement derived from the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: SOPs produce dynamic actin-based protrusions several cell diameters in length that physically interact with protrusions from neighbouring SOPs and epithelial cells.
source: SOPs in each row are actually separated by three to four epithelial cells, but SOPs produce dynamic actin-based protrusions several cell diameters in length that physically interact with protrusions from neighbouring SOPs and epithelial cells (Figure 2A left) (Cohen et al., 2010; Hunter et al., 2016; Renaud and Simpson, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2A and citations to previous work.

claim: When SOPs divide, they become spherical and protrusions are drastically reduced.
source: When SOPs divide, they become spherical and protrusions are drastically reduced (Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2—video 1.

claim: Overexpression of Rac1N17 results in shorter SOP protrusions than in the control.
source: Under these conditions, SOP protrusions were shorter than in the control (Figure 2C, p < 0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements of protrusion extension area shown in Figure 2C with statistical significance.

claim: SOPs with shorter protrusions divide more synchronously than in the control.
source: we observed that SOPs with shorter protrusions divide more synchronously than in the control (Figure 2E, mitotic wave rate 6.95 µm min–1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of division timing in rac1N17 conditions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In flies with short SOP protrusions, all SOPs in a row divided within one hour for all rows analysed.
source: Indeed, all SOPs in a row divided within one hour for all rows analysed (Figure 2E, Row 1 p < 0.0001; Row 2 p = 0.0292, Row 3 p = 0.0014, ANOVA, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the scaBP2 mutant, SOPs divided more simultaneously than in the control.
source: More importantly, in the scaBP2 mutant, SOPs divided more simultaneously than in the control (Row 1, p = 0.0015; Row 2, p = 0.0029; Row 3, p = 0.0014, ANOVA, Figure 3A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in multiple figures.

claim: Row one in scaBP2 divided in one-third of time taken for the control SOP row to divide.
source: For instance, Row one in scaBP2 divided in one-third of time taken for the control SOP row to divide, and the rate of the wave increased to 20.27 µm min1
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement comparing division timing between scaBP2 and control.

claim: The change in mitotic wave in scaBP2 was not associated with change in the cell fate of the sensory organs.
source: This change was not associated with change in the cell fate of the sensory organs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell fate marker analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference was found between scaBP2 and control SOP protrusions.
source: This Sca-mediated inhibition is not likely to be related to protrusion length shortening because no difference was found between scaBP2 and control SOP protrusions (Figure 2D and see Renaud and Simpson, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2D and citation to previous work.

claim: When sca expression was specifically downregulated using a conditional RNAi strategy between 12 and 19 hr APF, the mitotic wave was flattened.
source: In these conditions, as in null mutant, we again observed that the mitotic wave was flattened (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C; Row 1, p < 0.0001; Row 2, p = 0.69; Row 3, p = 0.003, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in multiple figures.

claim: Sca transported through cell protrusions specifically controls the wave of SOP mitoses along the rows.
source: These data indicate that Sca transported through cell protrusions specifically controls the wave of SOP mitoses along the rows.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined genetic and imaging experiments with sca mutants and RNAi.

claim: In Dl7/+ heterozygous background, no statistically significant reduction in the mitotic wave rate was observed.
source: We did not observe a statistically significant reduction in the mitotic wave rate in Dl7/+ SOPs (Figure 3D, p = 0.69, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No difference in the rate of the SOP division wave was observed in the scaBP2/+ heterozygous line.
source: Similarly, we did not observe any difference in the rate of the SOP division wave in the scaBP2/+ heterozygous line (Figure 3E, p = 0.71, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: When the gene dosage of both sca and Dl was reduced by half, the time-rank curves were flattened corresponding to a significant increase in the mitotic wave rate (from 3.14 to 43.35 µm min-1).
source: By contrast, when the gene dosage of both sca and Dl was reduced by half, the time-rank curves were flattened corresponding to a significant increase in the mitotic wave rate (from 3.14 to 43.35 µm min-1) (Figure 3F, p = 0.048, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 3F.

claim: sca and Dl genetically interact to control the SOP mitotic wave.
source: These results demonstrate that sca and Dl genetically interact, which suggests that these factors act in concert to control the SOP mitotic wave.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction experiments showing synergistic effects in double heterozygotes.

claim: Dl and Sca co-localise in vesicle-like structures inside the cytoplasm with Dl surrounding the Sca staining.
source: Indeed, we observed that Dl and Sca co-localise in vesicle-like structures inside the cytoplasm with Dl surrounding the Sca staining (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The wave of SOP mitoses along rows depends on an inhibitory signal transmitted by protrusions from the progenitors and is controlled by Dl and Sca proteins.
source: Altogether, our results show that the wave of SOP mitoses along rows depends on an inhibitory signal transmitted by protrusions from the progenitors and is controlled by Dl and Sca proteins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: In control pupae, the axon length varied along the antero-posterior axis, with neurons located at the extremities having shorter axons.
source: In control pupae, the axon length varied along the antero-posterior axis. Indeed, within a row, more the neurons were located at the extremities, the shorter their own axon.
evidence: This is supported by axon length measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In scaBP2 animals, the length of the axon along a row was significantly more homogeneous.
source: However, in scaBP2 animals, the length of the axon along a row was significantly more homogeneous (Figure 4B, p = 0.0232, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mitotic wave of SOP division controls axonogenesis timing.
source: Thus, the mitotic wave of SOP division controls axonogenesis timing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between mitotic wave disruption and axon length homogeneity.

claim: In control flies, 11% of ganglia analysed had a second medial commissure.
source: In 11% of ganglia analysed in control flies a second medial commissure was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 arrow).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from anatomical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In flies in which the mitotic wave was disrupted after sca downregulation (RNAi-sca), the percentage of ganglia with a medial commissure increased to 34%.
source: Interestingly, in flies in which the mitotic wave was disrupted after sca downregulation (RNAi-sca), this percentage increased to 34% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, p = 0.0002, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical significance shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In control flies, individual axon terminals have two main primary branches, an anterior branch that does not cross the midline and a posterior branch that crosses the midline.
source: We observed in control flies that individual axon terminals have two main primary branches, an anterior branch that does not cross the midline and a posterior branch that crosses the midline (Figure 4 C1 and C3 top panel).
evidence: This is supported by MCFO labeling data shown in Figure 4 C1 and C3.

claim: In RNAi-sca animals, axon terminals are more branched.
source: In RNAi-sca animals, we observed that axon terminals are more branched (Figure 4 C3 bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4 C3.

claim: The lengths of primary anterior and posterior branches of RNAi-sca axons were significantly shorter than those of control axons.
source: The lengths of primary anterior and posterior branches, between the root and the first branch point (Figure 4 C2), of RNAi-sca axons were significantly shorter than those of control axons (Figure 4D, p < 0.0001 and p = 0.0001 respectively, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The timing of axonogenesis is likely to be an important factor controlling axon branching.
source: As primary branches were shorter when SOP division occurred simultaneously on the notum, the timing of axonogenesis is likely to be an important factor controlling axon branching.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between synchronous SOP division and altered axon branching patterns.

claim: The order of birth of neurons in a given row contributes to the future connectivity of these neurons.
source: As such, our results led us to hypothesise that the order of birth of neurons in a given row contributes to the future connectivity of these neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed correlation between birth order and axon morphology.

claim: When the SOP mitotic wave was impaired, the number of air puffs required to elicit a leg response was significantly higher than in control flies.
source: When the SOP mitotic wave was impaired, after specific downregulation of sca during the wave, we found that the number of air puffs required to elicit a leg response was significantly higher than in control flies (Figure 5B, p = 0.028, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data with statistical significance shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The temporal order of neural precursor cells division impact on neuronal cell diversity and ultimately on behaviour.
source: Altogether, our results show that the temporal order of neural precursor cells division impact on neuronal cell diversity and ultimately on behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the combined results on mitotic wave, axon morphology, and behavior.

claim: Asynchrony in mitotic reactivation timing has been described in Drosophila larva neuroblasts.
source: Asynchrony in mitotic reactivation timing has been described in Drosophila larva neuroblasts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila neuroblast development.

claim: G2-arrested neuroblasts resume mitosis earlier than those in G0-arrest.
source: G2-arrested neuroblasts resume mitosis earlier than those in G0-arrest.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila neuroblast cell cycle regulation.

claim: The particular order of neuroblast division ensures that neurons form appropriate functional wiring.
source: As in our system, it has been proposed that this particular order of division ensures that neurons form appropriate functional wiring.
evidence: This is a proposal from previous work that is being compared to the current findings.

claim: Temporal processes controlling the wiring of peripheral receptors with the central nervous system have been described in the Drosophila eye.
source: It is relevant that other temporal processes controlling the wiring of peripheral receptors with the central nervous system have been described in the Drosophila eye, another highly organised structure (Fernandes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Fernandes et al., 2017.

claim: Temporal patterning mechanisms of neurogenesis could be more widespread than currently identified only in organised tissues.
source: It is conceivable that these temporal patterning mechanisms of neurogenesis, to date identified only in organised tissues, could be more widespread.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential generality of the findings.

claim: The cleaning reflex was significantly affected by altering the timing of microchaete precursor division in the dorsal thorax.
source: As such, it is remarkable that this fly behaviour was significantly affected by altering the timing of microchaete precursor division in the dorsal thorax.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral assay data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The SOP mitotic wave leads to a progressive neurogenesis along each row of microchaetes.
source: We show that the SOP mitotic wave leads to a progressive neurogenesis along each row of microchaetes.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between mitotic wave timing and axon length measurements.

claim: Progressive neurogenesis would likely induce a particular pattern of microchæte axon arrival in the thoracic ganglion required for the proper organisation of the neuropila in the central nervous system.
source: This, in turn, would likely induce a particular pattern of microchæte axon arrival in the thoracic ganglion required for the proper organisation of the neuropila in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observed progressive neurogenesis.

claim: When sca function was specifically downregulated during the SOP mitotic wave, axonogenesis occurs almost simultaneously in each row of microchaetes.
source: In any case, we show here that, when sca function was specifically downregulated during the SOP mitotic wave, axonogenesis occurs almost simultaneously in each row of microchaetes.
evidence: This is supported by the axon length homogeneity data in scaBP2 and RNAi-sca conditions.

claim: Simultaneous axonogenesis impairs the pattern of axon arrival into the ganglion leading to ectopic axon branching and changes in fly behaviour.
source: This certainly impairs the pattern of axon arrival into the ganglion leading to ectopic axon branching and changes in fly behaviour.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of altered axon morphology and impaired behavior.

claim: The anteromedial region corresponds approximately to the posterior limit of expression of the transcription factor BarH1.
source: Although the anteromedial region corresponds approximately to the posterior limit of expression of the transcription factor BarH1 (Sato et al., 1999), no factors specifically expressed in this region have yet been identified.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Sato et al., 1999.

claim: SOP0 may be selected by an emergent process related to cell-cell interaction in the epithelium, rather than by a passive pre-pattern.
source: Alternatively, as the location of SOP0 is modified when Sca function was impaired, an interesting possibility is that SOP0 is selected by an emergent process related to cell-cell interaction in the epithelium, rather than by a passive pre-pattern that organises the first events in the notum.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that SOP0 location changes in sca mutants.

claim: In proneural clusters, cells that express high levels of Dl and Sca become SOPs, while surrounding epithelial cells activate the N-pathway to prevent acquisition of a neural fate.
source: In proneural clusters, cells that express high levels of Dl and Sca become SOPs, while surrounding epithelial cells activate the N-pathway to prevent acquisition of a neural fate (Muskavitch, 1994; Renaud and Simpson, 2001; Buffin and Gho, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In eye and notum systems, Sca modulates N-activity at a long range.
source: In eye and notum systems, Sca modulates N-activity at a long range.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Scabrous function.

claim: During eye development, sca is expressed in intermediate clusters in the morphogenic furrow and transported posteriorly in vesicles through cellular protrusions to negatively control ommatidial cluster rotation.
source: Indeed, during eye development, sca is expressed in intermediate clusters in the morphogenic furrow and transported posteriorly in vesicles through cellular protrusions to negatively control ommatidial cluster rotation (Chou and Chien, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Chou and Chien, 2002.

claim: In the notum, SOP protrusions extend beyond several adjacent epithelial cells in which Dl and Scabrous are detected.
source: Similarly, in the notum, SOP protrusions extend beyond several adjacent epithelial cells in which Dl and Scabrous are detected (Renaud and Simpson, 2001 and this study).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and data from the current study.

claim: Sca, required to maintain SOPs in G2 arrest, is delivered focally through protrusions.
source: Since, we do not observe a reduction of the global level of sca expression associated with the wave progression, it is plausible that Sca, required to maintain SOPs in G2 arrest, is delivered focally through protrusions that are difficult to follow with in vivo analysis.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observations about Sca localization and protrusion function.

claim: G2 arrest in SOP cells is due to the downregulation of the promitotic factor Cdc25/String.
source: As in neuroblasts, G2 arrest in SOP cells is due to the downregulation of the promitotic factor Cdc25/String.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation in SOPs.

claim: Overexpression of string in SOPs induces a premature entry into mitosis.
source: Thus, overexpression of string in SOPs induces a premature entry into mitosis (Ayeni et al., 2016),
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Ayeni et al., 2016.

claim: Overexpression of negative regulators, like Wee1, maintain SOPs in arrest.
source: while overexpression of negative regulators, like Wee1, maintain these cells in arrest (Fichelson and Gho, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Fichelson and Gho, 2004.

claim: Sca may negatively regulate string expression, perhaps through the N-pathway.
source: Possibly Sca negatively regulates string expression, perhaps through the N-pathway that it is known to control the level of String (Deng et al., 2001; Krejcí et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The insulin-pathway regulates String level.
source: Alternatively, it has been recently shown that the insulin-pathway also regulates String level (Otsuki and Brand, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Otsuki and Brand, 2018.

claim: In muscle precursors, cell proliferation is induced by the insulin-mediated activation of the N-pathway.
source: Moreover, in muscle precursors, cell proliferation is induced by the insulin-mediated activation of the N-pathway (Aradhya et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Aradhya et al., 2015.

claim: Insulin may activate the N-pathway and Sca modulates this activation in the SOP system.
source: These observations raise the interesting possibility that, in our system, insulin activates the N-pathway and Sca modulates this activation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on previous findings in other systems.

claim: An essential condition for proper axon guidance is the competence of neurons to respond to environmental clues.
source: An essential condition for proper axon guidance is the competence of neurons to respond to these environmental clues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about axon guidance mechanisms.

claim: Neuron competence depends on the specific expression of transcriptional factors regulating their identity.
source: It is generally agreed that neuron competence depends on the specific expression of transcriptional factors regulating their identity (Petrovic and Hummel, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Petrovic and Hummel, 2008.

claim: The timing of neuron formation is a factor controlling their terminal morphology.
source: We show here that the timing of neuron formation is also a factor controlling their terminal morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing correlation between birth timing and axon morphology.

claim: The SOP mitotic wave induces a particular pattern of arrival of microchæte axons in the thoracic ganglion that establishes a specific framework of guidance cues on which circuits will be built.
source: We propose that the SOP mitotic wave induces a particular pattern of arrival of microchæte axons in the thoracic ganglion (Figure 6). This pattern establishes a specific framework of guidance cues on which circuits will be built and ultimately influencing an organism's behaviour.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: In addition to genetic factors, neurogenic timing is a parameter of development in the mechanisms controlling neural branching.
source: Our findings support the idea that, in addition to genetic factors, neurogenic timing is a parameter of development in the mechanisms controlling neural branching.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings.
